nodes.description: LDHD is a mitochondrial flavoenzyme of the vanillyl-alcohol-oxidase (FAD-binding type 4) family, peripherally associated with the inner membrane. With FAD, and in the mouse enzyme a manganese ion, in the active site it oxidises D-lactate to pyruvate and, with the same chemistry, other D-2-hydroxyacids that carry a small hydrophobic side chain; it does not act on L-lactate. Purified human LDHD passes the electrons directly to cytochrome c, so D-lactate oxidation enters the respiratory chain downstream of complexes I and III. Which face of the inner membrane the enzyme occupies is not settled: activity measurements in rat liver mitochondria placed it on the matrix side, whereas direct reduction of cytochrome c implies access to the intermembrane space. Its oligomeric state is also unsettled (monomer, dimer, tetramer and hexamer have each been reported). Biallelic pathogenic variants remove the dehydrogenase activity. Null alleles (a deletion of exons 1-7, a splice-donor duplication whose transcript is not detectable, and a frameshift in the last exon that replaces the C-terminal 53 residues, which include the manganese ligand Glu465, the catalytic His466 and the FAD-binding Asn502) abolish the protein or its active site. The five reported missense changes fall into two structural classes when placed on the mouse LDHD crystal structure with FAD, manganese and D-lactate bound: Arg370 and Trp374 line the substrate and flavin pocket (the Arg370 guanidinium is 2.9 angstroms from both carboxylate oxygens of D-lactate; Trp374 is 3.4 angstroms from FAD), whereas Thr463, Thr251 and Val69 are buried second-shell or core residues whose substitution destabilises the fold or the FAD site. In recombinant mouse enzyme all four tested substitutions lose about 90 percent of activity and are thermally destabilised, and the two threonine substitutions also lose FAD. The disease mechanism is therefore loss of function; nothing reported suggests a gain of function or a dominant-negative effect, and carrier parents are unaffected.

nodes.description: D-lactate is not a product of mammalian glycolysis. It is formed continuously in small amounts when the cytosolic glyoxalase system detoxifies methylglyoxal, a by-product of triose phosphate metabolism, and it also enters the body from fermented foods and from carbohydrate fermentation by intestinal bacteria. This load is normal; in LDHD deficiency it is the substrate that can no longer be cleared.

nodes.description: Homozygotes excrete a smaller fraction of filtered urate than their relatives, and their serum urate is raised. The proposed mechanism is anion exchange in the proximal tubule: D-lactate in the tubular lumen and cell is exchanged for urate, so the large D-lactate flux through the kidney drives urate back into blood. URAT1 (SLC22A12) is the known apical urate-anion exchanger of the human proximal tubule and is the obvious candidate, but no study of LDHD deficiency has tested which transporter is responsible.

NM_153486.3:c.1108C>T, homozygous in a consanguineous Bedouin-Israeli kindred with hyperuricemia and gout and the highest D-lactate concentrations reported. Arg370 lies in the C-terminal substrate-binding domain and is a direct substrate-binding residue: in the mouse structure 8JDE its guanidinium group is 2.9 angstroms from each carboxylate oxygen of D-lactate and 4.2 angstroms from the manganese ion, it is fully buried, and it is held by a salt bridge to Glu300.
